name: The Long Chronicle
sub: history and prehistory of the Hide, from the Cooling to the present count
epi: Nothing turned to look at us. I had thought something would.
preface:
Six documents, laid in the order of the ages they tell, from the first mark cut on the Cheek to the count that stands as I write. None of the hands is mine. I have changed nothing in them, and I have not made them agree. Where each came from:

[b]The Annal of the Cheek.[/b] Cut in the oldest lowland letters along a rib that stands out of the Moor's turf below the Jaw, under a hand's depth of warm ash; the Order's chronicle opens with a copy of it that no brother may show. I read the rib with a brush and my palm over four nights, and the ash was back over it by the fifth.

[b]Of the Founding, in Two Hands.[/b] A single leaf from the tally-room of the Fourth Stair at Nine Stairs, the two accounts glued face to face by the archivist who names himself at the foot; a sweeper carried it down the mountain in a bread-cloth and would not say which of the two hands he was afraid of.

[b]Dossier of the Wick-Binders.[/b] Three pieces sewn together at the front of the round-book of the tenders at Ashwake, whose rounds begin where the guild's book ends; the tender let me copy them while she wiped glass, and asked me not to read the middle piece aloud near a lit lamp.

[b]Muster of the Last Ascent.[/b] The roll and the steward's account were under the hearth-stone at Bellrest, where the monks keep what they will not burn; Brother Tenzar let me lift the stone, and counted the names after me, and got another.

[b]The Articles of the Knife and the Cord.[/b] The roll of the Concord lay on the bench in the empty keeper's hut at the Barrow Mouth, weighted with a stone that was warm; I took the roll and left the stone where it was.

[b]Survey of the Northern Walk.[/b] Sent down to the Chapter-House on Reliquary Avenue in the year it bears; the chalk was at the Prior's lintel when I came for it, and the Prior had not read past the Fen.

Each of these writers counted something, and each of them found the count wrong and went on counting. That is the whole of what they have in common, and it is why they lie together. Read them in their order. Do not total them.

pages.title: The Annal of the Cheek
pages.by: Cut in the oldest lowland letters along a rib that stands out of the Moor's turf below the Jaw, under a hand's depth of warm ash; the Order's chronicle opens with a copy of it that no brother may show. I read the rib with a brush and my palm over four nights, and the ash was back over it by the fifth.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The first hand[/color][/font_size]

One mark for each year since the breath went out past us. The others say there is no need of a count. I cut it. A thing counted is a thing kept, and I do not yet know what else is.

[b]1.[/b] We came out of the mouth onto the cheek, on the breath, and lay down in the ash. The ash was warm and is warm. Nothing turned to look at us. I had thought something would.

[b]2.[/b] The priest said the names of the god all winter and lost one in the spring. He does not know which. We have stopped asking him.

[b]3.[/b] The first of us died: a woman, of the cold, though the ground was warm. We put her in the ash. In the morning the ash over her was dished inward, like a cheek drawn in. We have not dug.

[b]4.[/b] Hands came up out of the ash to the east, the size of a man, with no arm to them. They walk on the fingers. They circle the fires at night and come in from behind. We keep our backs to the rib.

[b]5.[/b] Climbed the Jaw at dusk. From there the whole face can be seen, from the hollow of the eye to the ridge of the neck. It is not large. Inside, we had thought it was everything.

[b]6.[/b] The breath goes out past the camp toward the same quarter every night. Where it snags on a stone it thickens, and the stone speaks. Every stone speaks. Every ford. The small ones in them have not yet learned to be quiet.

[b]7.[/b] Nothing.

[b]8.[/b] On the white ridges to the north, far off: tall ones, standing where there was no one. They stand things up. A lintel was set over nothing at dusk, and in the morning there was a hall under it. They have not come down to us. We have not gone up.

[b]9.[/b] Some of us drank where the god's blood still runs out of the ash. Those who drank sat down in rows and waited. Where their own blood ran into the ash it made black glass. They stand up when three of us gather. We do not gather.

[b]11.[/b] A breath came through the camp with mouths in it and went out through the far wall of the tent without parting the cloth. It leaned away from the fire. We keep the fires low and we keep them lit.

[b]12.[/b] The tall ones cut marks on their stones, in rows, each mark the same distance from the last. I have cut my years so, on this rib, since the first. I did not know I had learned it from them until this year.

[b]13.[/b] The woman from the third year came up. Her head was on, but turned. The priest spoke to her. She went back down where the lid was dished, and the lid closed. We have mounded our dead since, and the mounds dish.

[b]15.[/b] Three tall ones came to the fires at the edge of the camp. Not the builders. These were hollow in the middle, as a reed is, and they spoke well, in our own tongue, and asked for the marrow of our dead, politely, and offered to carry the bones to the mounds for us after. We gave them nothing. They thanked us and went east. They called themselves the Ghauul. I set the word down as they said it, and my tongue is sore of it.

[b]16.[/b] A face of white clay came to the fire on wings, with a saint's look to it, and hung over the priest a long while, and went. He has not said the names since.

[b]18.[/b] Marks on the rib: eighteen. I cut them. Counted them this night: eighteen.

[b]19.[/b] The breath is weaker at the mouth than it was. The hollow of the eye to the south has filmed over, and the sea in it does not move like water. The ash is as warm as the first year.

[b]22.[/b] Nothing comes down from the ridges. The halls there are many now. We can see the doors by their lintels at dusk, in a row along the white, each lower than a man. They light no fires.

[b]24.[/b] The young man Orrin went north to the ridges against the priest's word and came back in the spring with no bread and no cold on him, and with a word in his mouth that he could not stop saying. The builders' name for themselves. He said it to the fire and to the children and to the dead on the mounds until he had no other word left. I cut it on the rib here, below this year, as he said it.

[ … ]

By morning the rib had closed over the cut, as skin closes over a splinter, and Orrin was quiet, and has stayed quiet. The mark of the year is still there.

[b]25.[/b] Counted the marks: twenty-six. I have cut twenty-five. I did not cut the other. I cut nothing to close this year but these words.

[b]26.[/b] There was a thin one at the edge of the firelight at dusk, standing where the hands circle, not circling. It had a finger up, and it moved the finger along us, one, and one, and one, as I move the knife along the rib. In the morning we were one fewer, and nobody could say who. The priest says the hands took one. The hands take loudly.

[b]27.[/b] Orrin spoke, once. He said the thin one has a name in the builders' mouths, and said it, and was quiet again. Ykkoth-Taal. I have cut it once. I will not cut it twice.

[b]28.[/b] Counted the marks: twenty-eight. Twenty-eight. The year closes.

[b]31.[/b] The halls on the ridges have a hall under them now; the lintels we can see are the upper lintels only. The builders go in at dusk and fewer come out. They are not fewer. I have watched. They are the same number, and fewer.

[b]33.[/b] A ring of stones with teeth stood round a pit in the ash below the Jaw at dawn, where no pit was. Nobody of ours set it. The tall ones stood on the ridge all that day, at a distance, not coming down, facing it. The priest says they raised it. I say they faced it as we did, and will say no more.

[b]36.[/b] The breath is weaker still. The small ones in the stones are quieter. We thought we would be glad.

[b]40.[/b] Counted the marks: forty-one. The forty-first is under the thirty-third, cut smaller, with a tool that is not mine. I have laid my knife against it. It is cut from the other side of the rib.

[b]41.[/b] I will cut no mark this year, to make the count right. It is a year. I have cut nothing.

[b]42.[/b] Forty-two. The rib has it right without me.

[b]47.[/b] A pilgrim who had drunk of the blood came and knelt at the edge of the ash and did not stand when three of us gathered. He is kneeling there still. There are more of them every year, and the first was a man I knew.

[b]50.[/b] Half a hundred. The priest is dead. We laid him in a mound and the mound dished, and he has not come up. The names of the god are gone out of the camp with him, except the three the children keep, which are short.

[b]53.[/b] The tall ones have begun to lie down. We see them at dusk go into the long low doors and not come out, one at each dusk. They are not dying. Orrin says they are being finished. He has said more this year than in twenty. I would rather he had not.

[b]58.[/b] Something walked up the road out of the south at dusk, past the camp, toward the mouth, against the breath. Gaunt, hooded, with a staff, not stopping. Where it passed, the kneeling ones lay down on their faces, and two of the hands, and old Hesk at the fire, who was not dead, and they stayed so. It did not look at us. It was going up. Orrin said the builders' name for it, Ath-Sorrauun, and said the builders had seen it walking before the breath went out, and that it had been walking then. I have cut the name because Orrin asked me to, and because I think he will not ask again.

[b]61.[/b] Counted the marks. I will not write the figure. It is higher than my age, and I was a man when we came out.

[b]66.[/b] The ash is as warm as the first year. The breath is less. The sea in the eye has a skin on it. The halls on the ridge are dark at dusk now, every lintel, and I have not seen a tall one standing in nine years. The halls are still there. Orrin says the halls are the tall ones: that they lay down, and the halls are what they are now, and that the lintels are counting still, in notches, from the other side. I have asked him to stop.

[b]70.[/b] Seventy. Orrin went up to the ridges in the autumn to lie down in a door. He said it was his count that was wrong, not mine. He did not come back, and I have not gone to see which hall.

[b]74.[/b] A boy, Tam's son, has begun to cut marks on the far side of the rib. He has cut four. I did not teach him. I asked him what he counted. He said: the ones that are not here.

[b]80.[/b] I am old. The breath is a draught now where it was a wind. The warm has not gone out of the ash. I put my palm on the rib tonight to feel the marks I cut, and I can feel more than I cut, and on the far side under my fingers I can feel the boy's, and they are more than four.

[b]83.[/b] The count will be kept. Tam's son swears it. Teach it to one, and have that one teach it, and let the one who keeps it know what I knew: the marks are more than the years. Cut your mark anyway. A thing counted is

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]The first hand stops there, mid-line, at the eighty-third mark. What follows is cut smaller, by the hand that cut the far side.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]84.[/b] He is in the mound by the Jaw. The lid dished the first night and has not opened. I have cut the eighty-fourth. I have counted the rib. I will say the figure once, since he would not: ninety-one.

[b]90.[/b] Nothing comes down from the ridges. The lintels can be seen at dusk in a row, lower than a man, and under them, when the breath is quite still, the row of them again, lower, as a face is under water.

[b]97.[/b] The sea in the eye is quite still. The breath is a draught. The ash is warm. The marks on both sides of the rib are more than the years. I have stopped cutting my own. The count goes on without me, a mark a year, on the near side, in the first hand.

[b]100.[/b] One hundred. I have counted the rib this night, and I set the figure down because he would not and I said I would: one hundred and nine. I have put the knife in the ash at the foot of the rib. Whoever takes it up, cut your mark. What is counted is kept. What else is kept I do not know, and it is still warm.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the first to keep the count, and the second[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Of the Founding, in Two Hands
pages.by: A single leaf from the tally-room of the Fourth Stair at Nine Stairs, the two accounts glued face to face by the archivist who names himself at the foot; a sweeper carried it down the mountain in a bread-cloth and would not say which of the two hands he was afraid of.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [i]The Foundation Account, as it is read at the Feast of the Laying in every house of the Order, is the upper hand. The lower hand is the deposition of a mason of Cold Adit, taken by the reeve's clerk there in the nine hundred and seventh year, which I found as the backing-board of the Account's binding, glued face down. I have laid them on one leaf. My note is at the foot.[/i]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The Foundation Account[/color][/font_size]

In the nine hundredth year of the Breath, by the count the Mother gave us, nine brothers came up out of the lowlands into the Ossa carrying the bones of the lowland dead in sacks, because the lowlands mounded what should stand, and the mounds dished, and what came up out of them came up wrong.

Let it be written that they were led, and by whom: by the Bearing Mother, whose bone is the Ossa, who drew them up the white as a cord draws a weight. The ninth brother, whose name the Rule does not write, carried the cord.

They came to the lintels at dusk. Let it be written that the halls stood open, and swept, and empty, and that no hand had made them but hers, and that [ … ] had left them so. The niches were cut to her measure, which is not ours, that we might be humbled lying in them. The stairs were cut to her stride, which is not ours, that we might climb on our hands, as the penitent climbs. The marks on the lintels were her first Count, cut by her own finger before any brother could count, and the brothers read them and found them to be nine, and nine, and nine; and so nine houses, and nine stairs.

Let it be written that the lowest door was shut, and that Haddo, a Tithed of the lowlands who had come up with the nine as their carrier, laid his hand upon its lintel and tithed to the Mother his finger, the ninth, and the door stood open, and he was given a hall. In the lowland mouths he is Haddo Nine-Fingers. In ours he has no name but a number, which is open still, and the hall is the Hall of Haddo under the Fourth Stair, where the Brothers of the Well draw what she gives.

Let it be written that the brothers laid the first bones on the first night in the first niches, and said over each a name or the name of the bone, and counted the wall, and the wall was at its count. Let it be written that on the second morning the wall was one higher, and that this was the first of her gifts, and that the brothers gave thanks.

Let it be written that we stood beside her when she fell and will stand beside her when she rests; that the Order is as old as the falling and came to its house in the nine hundredth year; that the halls were hers and are ours; and that nothing was taken, because there was no one to take from.

Let the lowest door stay shut.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The deposition of Wat Carrow, mason[/color][/font_size]

I am Wat Carrow, mason, of Cold Adit, and I was hired in the nine hundred and first year with six of my gang by the brothers on the white, to wall. I set this down before the reeve because I am paid and have come down, and because the brothers asked me to forget it, and a mason is paid to remember a wall.

We were hired to shut doors, not to open them. There were seven of us to wall and we walled thirty-one doors in six years, every one below the fourth stair, every one too low for a man and too wide for two.

The halls were not empty. I say what I mean. There was nobody in them. But a hall that has been lain in is not empty, as a bed is not empty in the morning, and every long niche below the fourth stair was worn smooth for shoulders too far from the head-end, and was warm. We put our hands in them. You could not help it.

The lintels were bone. Not stone cut like bone: bone, with the grain running through it from the wall into the wall, so that lintel and jambs and sill were one piece and had grown. I have set lintels forty years. These were not set. The brothers said they were the Mother's. I will not say they were not. I will say the brothers paid us extra to cut the marks off them.

The marks. Every lintel below the fourth stair carries rows of notches a thumb apart, cut from both faces, so that each notch goes in from the front and in from the back and they meet in the middle. We cut them off thirty-one lintels with cold chisels. The dust came out warm. By morning the dust on the floor under each lintel lay in rows, a thumb apart. We swept it. It came back. On the fourth morning the brothers stopped us sweeping and had us wall the doors with the dust lying as it lay, and gave us a coin each to say the lintels were plain.

Over the lowest door, which we walled on the last day of the sixth year, the notches made a word in the notch-letters, which the brothers' ninth man could read and would not. The young brother who held the lamp read it to me under his breath, to show that he could, and I set it here as he said it, because he is dead and the word is not: Khurr-Ossat. It is what they called themselves, the ones who grew the lintels. He said it meant the ones who stood up, or the bone's own hands, or the ones between; he did not know which, and said the lintel knew. He said the brothers are forbidden it on the stair, and that the ninth man had said it once, at the lowest door, and the door had opened.

Haddo. They say he gave the finger. I was there with the hod. He put his hand up to the lintel to feel the notches, as a man will, and the bone closed on the ninth finger the way a knee closes, and held, and he did not cry out until it was done, and then he said the word that was on the lintel, not the Mother's name, and the door below, which we had walled that morning with good stone and lime, was open, and the stone we had walled it with stood in a stack to the side, dressed, as if we had never set it. He has a hall. He does not go into it.

The count. The brothers counted the niches of the lowest hall with us by: nineteen. We counted twenty. We counted together: twenty. Nobody could say which had been missed. I have laid a thousand courses and I can count to twenty.

The ninth man. He led them up the white with a cord, and he had no face that I could bring to mind once he had turned away, and he was tall for a brother, and his stair was the one we could not walk, and I never once saw him on his hands.

I was paid in salt and a number. I do not know my number. The brothers do. I would like it written that I did honest work and would not do it again, and that the thirty-one doors I walled below the fourth stair are walled still, and that there are thirty-two walls.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The archivist's note[/color][/font_size]

I have laid the two hands on one leaf because they were already on one leaf, back to back, and had been for eleven hundred years and more, and I do not think the binder who glued the deposition face-down meant to destroy it. He meant to hide it where it would last. That is a thing a brother does.

Of the Account: a word is scraped from the fourth line in every copy I have handled, in the same place, and the vellum under the scraping is worn as if by a thumb. The deposition supplies the word. I have not written it into the gap. It stands nowhere on this leaf but in the mason's line, in his spelling, and I ask the Wardens after me to leave it there, since it has lain on the leaf in the dark all this while and done no harm I can measure.

Of the deposition: I have checked the mason's measures against the lowest hall. The doors are as he gives them, to a thumb. The notches are not on the lintels. The dust is on the floor, in rows, a thumb apart. The sweepers do not sweep the lowest hall. I asked why. I was told that no one does.

He gives thirty-one doors walled and thirty-two walls. I have counted the walls below the fourth stair. I will not set down the figure, since the Rule says nothing is laid without its name and I cannot give this one a name. I will say it is not thirty-one.

The Account is read at the Feast and the deposition is not. I do not propose to change that. I propose that this leaf be laid in the niche under the Account's number, face out, as the Rule requires, so that it is counted. Let the Wardens after me choose. I have chosen to the extent of writing this, which is further than the binder went, and I am aware of the distance.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Archivist of the Fourth Stair, in the two thousand and sixty-first year of the Breath, root nine, which I set down because the Warden will ask[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Dossier of the Wick-Binders
pages.by: Three pieces sewn together at the front of the round-book of the tenders at Ashwake, whose rounds begin where the guild's book ends; the tender let me copy them while she wiped glass, and asked me not to read the middle piece aloud near a lit lamp.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The writ[/color][/font_size]

Writ of the Wardens in Agreement, given at Nine Stairs in the eleven hundred and seventh year of the Breath, against the guild that calls itself the Wick-Binders, and against every lamp of theirs.

Let it be written what they are. A guild of the lowlands, of the Tithed, in number uncertain, having its house at the Ashwake stones, which sets glass about a flame that is not a flame. The flame is a soul.

Let it be written what they do. When one of the Tithed falls on the road, the anima goes down, as the Rule teaches, into the Last Breath, and is carried, and the Mother receives what is finished. The binders stand at the lantern-stones with their glass and their wick and ask it to look back. What looks back, they keep.

The reasons are these.

[b]I.[/b] That the anima is not theirs. It is the Mother's, as the frame is, lent for a life.

[b]II.[/b] That a soul kept is a count that cannot close. The Count rises every year in every house; the talliers carry what is open; a flame in glass is a figure that will never be reduced, and every lantern on the road is one more.

[b]III.[/b] That they take a little of the one the flame follows, each time it carries him home, and burn it, so that the one who walks beside a lantern comes to the Mother less than he was and lighter than his frame.

[b]IV.[/b] That they keep what should go down, and that what should go down and does not is what stands up wrong in the mounds. The lowlands say the barrows rise of themselves. The Wardens say the barrows rise because the going-down has been made a thing that may be refused.

[b]V.[/b] That they have asked the flames what is below, and written the answers in their wick-book, and read them to pilgrims at the stones. This is the gravest of the reasons. The Wardens in agreement will not set down what is written, and order it unwritten.

Let the sentence be this. The guild's glass to be broken by the knights of the Kostyak, with the standing dead to carry the pieces up the stair. The binders to be brought up the white to the grate, and entered, and given numbers, that their names may close. The wick-book to be brought up the white unread, and read by one Warden alone, and laid under the Ninth Stair with the weights. The flames, when the glass is broken, to be let go down, and a brother to stand at each stone and count what goes.

The lantern-stones to be left standing. The tenders to be left. A lamp of the Order's own, of marrow-tallow, to be hung on each.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— under the hands of the Wardens in agreement, the walls standing at their count[/color][/i][/right]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The reply of the guild[/color][/font_size]

To the Wardens on the white, from the binders at the stones, by the hand of Mael, who bound the first, and is old.

You say we ask the flames to look back. We do not. Nobody can be asked to. Hear what a binder does, since you have sentenced it without hearing. We stand at the stone with the glass open and the wick dry, and we keep still. Most of what goes out past us does not look back. It goes where you say, down, and we have never once held it, and could not. A few look back. It is not love; we have asked them; it is wanting to see who is still walking. Those few we give a wick to. The wick is a name. The glass is only to keep the wind off, because it is the breath they ride, the long one, which has not finished leaving, which your lowlands call the Last Breath and your inner stair calls Hau'Nuulh, and which we call by neither, because it answers to neither.

You say we take a little each time. We do. The road home costs. Nobody else pays it. You would have the fallen stay fallen and be carried up your stair in sacks. We would have them stand up in the warm ash with one thing fewer, and walk. Ask the road which it prefers.

You say what should go down must go down. We asked them, Wardens. That is the charge you will not write, so I will. We asked the flames what is below, every one, for sixty years, and wrote it in the wick-book, and I will set here what they said, because you are about to make it so that nobody can.

They say: it is not down.

They say: there is no one at the bottom. Not the Mother. Not the Maiden. Not the Crone. Nothing receives. The breath goes out of the mouth and keeps going, and they ride it a while, and then it is wide, and it is not looking, and they are in it, and nothing notices that they are.

They say: it does not take them. It does not want them. It is weather.

They say: the ones who look back are the ones who understood what they were being carried into, and would rather be a flame in a tender's glass on a cold road than be in a place that does not know they have arrived.

That is the whole of what the wick-book holds. There is nothing of yours in it. There is nothing of the Mother's gift in it, which you count every Feast and will not name. We do not know what the gift is either, Wardens. We only know where your dead are not.

My daughter was the first. She asked. She has followed me forty years, a little behind, a little to one side, and she has carried me home eleven times, and I am lighter and she is heavier, and tonight she is on the stone behind me reading this over my shoulder, as she does, and she has just leaned. She agrees with none of it. She says the dark down there sang.

Break the glass. The flames will not go where you send them. They did not go where they were sent the first time. They will go where they choose, and they have chosen the road, and you will hang marrow lamps on empty stones for a thousand years while the road lights itself behind you.

Dust on the glass. Wipe it. It is someone.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Mael, binder, at Ashwake; and under it, in a smaller hand pressed in soot: and his daughter, who does not agree[/color][/i][/right]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Lanterns lit in the last year of the book[/color][/font_size]

From the wick-book of the guild, the eleven hundred and forty-ninth year, being the last leaf written in it.

[b]The Ridge above Ashwake, the far stone.[/b] A ridge-warden who fell at his post in the thaw. Looked back for a boot on the stones. Wick by Mael's daughter, Mael's hand being past it. A small bell hung in the glass cracked in the hanging and will not be mended; it sighs when the breath is up. Chose: no one yet. It waits on the stone, and hums.

[b]The Barrow ring stone.[/b] A digger of Widow's Lane, from under a lid. Looked back for the sound of his own spade, which was still going. Wick by Hesk. Chose a child of nine on the road with her mother. The mother tried to send it back to the stone. It would not go.

[b]The crossing below the Jaw.[/b] A penitent of the Wound with his sleeves stiff to the elbow. Looked back for the litany. Wick by Osk. Chose the knight who had come down the white to break our glass, and goes with him, a little behind, and the knight has not turned round.

[b]The Fen stair.[/b] No one. A dry wick stood on the stone nine nights and took no flame, and on the tenth morning the glass was warm and the wick was black and there was nothing in it, and it follows the tender on her round, and she has stopped looking to see.

[b]The Heath stone, outside the ring of the carcasses, where no lamp will go in.[/b] A carter. Looked back for his cart. Wick by Osk. Chose no one. Stands at the ring's edge facing in. Each round it is a pace nearer the ring than the tender set it.

[b]The grate stone under the white, which we have never hung before.[/b] A novice of the Order who fell on the low road with the bone-sacks. Looked back for his count: he had an open count in his head and would not go down with it unclosed. Wick by Mael's daughter. The knights took the glass up the white. The stair's lamps burn marrow. This one burns a boy, and they have hung it, and they know.

[b]Ashwake, the home stone.[/b] Mael. Fell at the stone in the autumn with the glass open and the wick dry, and looked back. His daughter wicked him. He is on the home stone. He has chosen the tender who writes this, and I have not turned round.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]The knights came up the Ridge road in the first frost with their dead behind them, forty, which I counted, and the glass is broken on every stone from the Jaw to the Fen stair, and I have swept it, and I am to write what went where. Nothing went down. I watched. The flames stood a while in the cold where the glass had been, and leaned, and went along the road a little behind the knights, a little to one side, and the knights have not turned round, and the brother who was to count what went down wrote a figure and scratched it out and asked for the sweeping. This is the last leaf. I am the tender of the Ashwake round. The round-book begins on the next.[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Muster of the Last Ascent
pages.by: The roll and the steward's account were under the hearth-stone at Bellrest, where the monks keep what they will not burn; Brother Tenzar let me lift the stone, and counted the names after me, and got another.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The roll[/color][/font_size]

Roll of the An-Vhar'ith who go up the Stair on the day of the Last Ascent, in the four hundred and fourth year of the Climb, which is one bell for each year hung in the Hollow, and which the lowlands count as the one thousand four hundred and third year of their Breath, a count we do not keep, since what they count from is what we are climbing out of.

Mustered at the foot of the Stair at first grey by the steward, who stays, and does not go up, and keeps the hearth, which has not gone out since the god died.

[b]Of the great bell:[/b] Pema Choden, Abbess of the Bell. Goes up first. Carries the clapper, wrapped.

[b]Of the Hollow, the ringers, nine:[/b] Norbu; Sonam Dorje; Lhakpa; Tsering the elder; Tsering the younger; Rinchen Wangmo; Dawa; Jigme Lhundrup; Yeshe. Go up second, after the ringing, leaving the ropes tied off.

[b]Of the Breath-Caves, the holders, seven:[/b] Karma; Dechen; Phurba; Tashi Gyaltsen; Nyima; Ani Dolkar; Pasang, who has held one breath since the Feast of Flags and has not yet let it go. Go up third, in silence.

[b]Of the Hall of Threads, the thread-wardens, five:[/b] Gyurme; Chime Lhamo; Tenpa; Sangye; Dorjee Rabten. Go up fourth, with the threads paid out behind them from the loft, that the Hall may know where they are.

[b]Of the wrights, three:[/b] Ugyen the Chime-Wright; Wangdu; Kalsang. Go up fifth, having lit the spires. The two old wrights, Thubten and Lobsang, stay, being past the Stair, and are not on this roll.

[b]Novices, eight:[/b] Tenzin; Pemba; Dolma; Namgyal; Lhamo the small; Nhaal; Chophel; Tsomo; Mingyur. Go up sixth, hand to belt.

[b]The Abbot of the Stair,[/b] whose given name went into the first bell. Goes up last, alone, carrying nothing.

[b]Mustered to go up: thirty-four. Staying below: the steward, two wrights, the hearth-boy. Thirty-eight at the foot of the Stair.[/b]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The steward's account[/color][/font_size]

Set down at the hearth at Bellrest on the night of the Last Ascent and the eight nights after, by the steward, for whoever comes up the pass and finds the hearth lit and nobody at it.

[b]First grey.[/b] I mustered at the foot of the Stair by the roll above, which I wrote the night before from the Abbot's list. The Abbot's list had thirty-four. I counted thirty-four at the foot, by head, twice. I read the roll aloud and every name answered. I have read the roll since, nine times. It has thirty-five names. The one I cannot place is written in my own hand between Lhamo the small and Chophel: Nhaal. There is no novice of that name. There was no one at the foot of the Stair who answered to it, and yet when I read the roll aloud every name answered, and I heard no silence. The hearth-boy says a voice answered from higher up the Stair than anyone had yet climbed. He is nine, and I have written it.

[b]The spires.[/b] The wrights lit the Field at first light, every spire, with the warmth they have been borrowing from the long breath for this since the Climb began. They burn pale and give no smoke. The Stair could be seen from the hearth the whole way up to where the cloud sits, a thread of lit brass, and above the cloud the summit, and the great bell in its frame, which I have seen on every clear morning of my life and which that morning I could not look at long.

[b]The ringing.[/b] The nine went into the Hollow and rang the years. There are four hundred and four bells hung there, one for each year since the first of us set foot to the first riser, and the nine rang every one in its order, from the first bell, which is small and has the Abbot's given name cast inside it, to the four hundred and fourth, which was hung on the eve and had never been struck. It took from first light until the sun stood over the Glass Pass. I counted the strokes, because it is my office to count what is spent. Four hundred and four. Then the ringers tied off the ropes and came out and went up, and the bells went on.

I set that down plainly, as I would set down a short measure of barley. The ringers were on the second flight, with the ropes tied off, and the bells in the Hollow went on ringing the years in their order, from the first, a second time, with no hand on any rope. The wrights say the bronze figures they cast to sleep among the bells are there to keep the harmony, not to ring. The bronze did not move; I went in to see; the ropes hung still, and the bells rang. I counted. Four hundred and five.

[b]The Abbess's doctrine,[/b] which she gave at the foot of the Stair before she went up first, and which I set down so that it is somewhere. That the lowlands are wrong about the mouth. That the mouth on the Moor where the Tithed came out was the mouth of the dying, and is nearly shut; that a dead thing's mouth falls open; that the sky over An-Vhar is where it has fallen open, and that the breath which has not finished leaving goes out through it and may be followed; and that she would go up to the lip and ring the great bell once, so that whatever is outside would know that someone was coming out, and would turn to look. She said: it will turn and look at us. We will be the first thing it has ever looked at. Then she went up, with the clapper wrapped in her robe.

[b]The going up.[/b] They went in their orders, as the roll gives: the holders without a breath among them, the thread-wardens paying out their threads from the loft so that the Hall might know, the novices hand to belt, nine of them on the first flight by my count, where I had mustered eight. The same number, and one more. I did not go up to count again. The Abbot went last, at the ninth hour, alone, carrying nothing, and bowed to the hearth before he went, which an Abbot does not do.

[b]Dusk.[/b] At dusk the great bell rang once.

I have kept a hearth forty years and I know what a bell is. It was no bell of the Hollow. It came down the Stair the way cold comes down it, and every spire in the Field leaned away from the summit at once, and the hearth, which has not gone out since the god died, lay flat on the stone and stood up again. The hearth-boy says the stroke was answered. I did not hear an answer. I heard the stroke, and then I heard the Hollow: every bell of the four hundred and five ringing at once, not in order, flat, by one breath, as if each had been struck a little late. They have rung flat since. The wrights say every bell on the Hide rings flat now by that one breath, and that it is our doing. I set down that I do not know, and that I would rather it were not.

[b]The threads.[/b] On the second morning the thread-wardens' threads, which had been paid out up the Stair and were taut at dusk, lay slack on the risers all the way up to the cloud, and the hearth-boy and I wound them in. They came in the whole way with no weight on the end, and the ends were not cut and not broken, and were warm.

[b]The summit.[/b] On the seventh morning the cloud lifted and I took the Abbot's far-glass to the Cloud-Shelf. There is one standing at the top, by the great bell, with a hand on its rim. He has stood so three clear mornings. The frost does not settle on him. The bell has no clapper that I can see. He is the colour of the bell. I could make out no one else at the summit, and I looked a long while, and I set down that the sky over the summit is not the colour of the sky over the pass, and that I have looked at it as long as I am going to.

[b]Stores.[/b] Barley to the spring. Dung for the hearth to the spring. Thirty-four bowls, which I have put away. Thirty-five robes hang folded in the loft, by the roll. I folded thirty-four.

[b]Of the count.[/b] I have mustered this house forty years and never been out by one. I set down that the roll is right and I am wrong, since the Stair agreed with the roll and the hearth-boy heard the name answer. I set down that I do not know what went up the Stair that I had not mustered, or whether it went up at all, or was already there and the roll only noticed it. I set down that the bells ring flat, that the one at the top is the colour of the bell, and that I keep the hearth.

The lowlanders will say the sky swallowed them. The Abbess said it would turn and look. I say that on the ninth night I went to the foot of the Stair with a lamp and looked up it as far as the cloud, and the Stair had one riser fewer than it had on the morning I mustered, and I know the Stair, and I will not go up it to count

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]The steward's hand ends on the ninth night. Below it, in the hearth-boy's letters, large: HE WENT UP TO COUNT. THE HEARTH IS LIT. I HAVE PUT HIS NAME ON THE ROLL. IT IS AT ITS COUNT.[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: The Articles of the Knife and the Cord
pages.by: The roll of the Concord lay on the bench in the empty keeper's hut at the Barrow Mouth, weighted with a stone that was warm; I took the roll and left the stone where it was.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] Concord between the Pale Order of the Ossa and the Brotherhood of the Precious Wound, touching the dead of the Barrow lands and the Barrow road, sworn at the Grieving Stone at the Barrow Mouth in the two thousand three hundred and fortieth year of the Breath, which the Order chose for its root. Under the year the Brotherhood's clerk wrote a figure of his own count, from the first cup, which the first keeper could not read and did not copy.

[b]I.[/b] THE DEAD OF THE BARROW LANDS AND OF THE BARROW ROAD, FROM THE JAW TO THE CROSSING AT FOUR WENTS, BELONG TO THESE TWO HOUSES AND TO NO OTHER, THE FRAME TO THE BEARING MOTHER AND THE FLESH TO THE MAIDEN, AND NEITHER HOUSE SHALL CARRY A WHOLE BODY OFF THE ROAD.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Kept nine years. In the tenth a knight carried a whole man up the white in a sack, saying the flesh had gone to dust in the night and there was nothing to part. The penitents dug where he had lain. The ground was wet.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: Nobody carries whole bodies now. They are not whole when found.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]II.[/b] WHAT IS WARM IS THE MAIDEN'S AND WHAT IS COLD IS THE MOTHER'S. A BODY IS COLD WHEN A BROTHER OF THE ORDER MAY LAY HIS BARE PALM ON THE BREASTBONE FOR THE SAYING OF THE MOTHER'S NINE NAMES, SLOWLY, AND FEEL NOTHING.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: The knights say the names quickly. The penitents say them slowly on the knights' behalf. In my twentieth year the houses agreed a pace, beaten on the Stone with a stick, and it is my office to beat it, and I do.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: The dead of the Barrow lands keep their warmth longer than they did. I beat the pace. The knights lay the palm. It is warm at nine names, and at nine times nine. The Brotherhood takes them. The Order has begun to bring a brother who, by his own account, feels nothing in his hand, and lays that.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: The Stone is warm at nine names. I have laid my palm on it.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]III.[/b] THE MARROW GOES WITH THE BONE. THE BLOOD GOES WITH THE FLESH. THE TEETH ARE BONE. THE HAIR AND THE NAILS ARE THE MAIDEN'S.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Broken on the marrow in the first winter, both ways. The Brotherhood cracks the long bones warm and the Order says the marrow was theirs. The Order renders the marrow for its lamps and the Brotherhood says it was given to the Maiden by the man's own heat. I wrote both. Each asked me to strike the other.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: The marrow of the Barrow dead sets like wax now before the bone is cold. Neither house will take it set. It lies in the ditches below the Stone. It is warm.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: The teeth. The Order came for a tally of the teeth in my ninth year. The figure was higher than the jaws allowed. They called it the gift and wrote it. I have the jaws.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]IV.[/b] THE PARTING SHALL BE DONE BY THE KNIGHT'S KNIFE AND RECEIVED BY THE PENITENT'S HANDS, AND NEITHER HOUSE SHALL PART ALONE, NOR SING WHILE THE KNIFE IS IN.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: The penitents sing. They say the Maiden cannot be kept waiting in silence. The knights count aloud under the singing. I have stood between them with the roll and could not have said which was the prayer.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: In my thirty-first year a knight parted alone by the Turned Mound at dusk, and the body sat up under the knife and turned to each road in turn. He finished. He brought me the cord to witness. It had the right count. It had the right count twice, and the third time more, and he took it away up the white without the bones.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: They part together again. Not by the articles. Because neither will stand alone over what the Mound gives up now.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]V.[/b] NO KNIGHT'S NAME SHALL BE SUNG IN THE BROTHERHOOD'S LITANIES, AND NO BROTHER OF THE WOUND SHALL BE ENTERED IN THE ORDER'S BOOK UNDER A NUMBER.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Broken on both sides within the year. Both deny it to me yearly, standing on the Stone, and I write that they deny it.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: The Hermano Mayor asked me in my twelfth year what his number was. I told him I did not know. He said the knights say it under the singing, and that it adds to nine, and that he is afraid of its closing.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: They sing the knights by number now. The knights answer to it.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]VI.[/b] THE ORDER'S BONE-CARTS AND THE BROTHERHOOD'S CARTS SHALL PASS ON THE BARROW ROAD WITH THE BONE-CART TO THE EAST, AND NEITHER SHALL HALT WITHIN SIGHT OF THE OTHER.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Kept. Nobody wants to look.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: A cart halted in sight of the other in my fourth year, in the lane below the Stone, and both houses stood off it, and neither would go to it, and it stood seven days, and the singing in it stopped on the sixth, and on the eighth it was gone, and the ruts went no further than the place it had stood.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]VII.[/b] ONE OF THE BARROW DEAD WHO RISES WRONG SHALL BELONG TO WHICHEVER HOUSE REACHES IT FIRST, AND THE OTHER SHALL NOT CONTEST, AND THE LIDS SHALL BE LEFT AS THEY LIE.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Both houses keep a runner at the Barrow Mouth now, to watch the lids for the dishing. The runners have become friends. Their houses do not know.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: The runners are dead, both, in the same winter, under the same lid, and the lid is dished, and neither house will open it to see whose they are.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: The lids lift now. From below. Not far: a hand's breadth, at the dished hour, every mound in Widow's Lane at once, and set down again. Neither house reaches them first. Both arrive after.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]VIII.[/b] THE BROTHERHOOD SHALL LEAVE NO BREAD ON THE ORDER'S MILESTONES, AND THE ORDER SHALL TAKE NO BREAD FROM THEM.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: The bread is left. The bread is taken. Both deny it on the Stone. I ate one of the loaves. It was sweet and I slept well and I have not done it since.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: The bread is left. Something takes it that is not the Order. The knights have begun to leave a bone on the milestone in its place, counted, and it is gone by morning too.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: There is a loaf on the milestone below the Stone that has lain there eleven years and is warm.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]IX.[/b] THIS CONCORD SHALL LIE WITH THE KEEPER OF THE GRIEVING STONE, WHO IS OF OURS, AND SHALL BE READ AT THE STONE EACH YEAR AT THE THAW BEFORE A KNIGHT AND A PENITENT, AND THE HOUSE THAT DOES NOT SEND SHALL BE HELD TO HAVE BROKEN ALL THE ARTICLES.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: Read thirty-one years. I was sworn at the signing, of neither house, as the article has it, and I have read it thirty-one thaws, and both houses have sent, and the knight stands to the east and the penitent to the west and I stand on the Stone. The hollow in the Stone holds rain and does not freeze. I am old. Tobbe takes the roll.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Second keeper: Read thirty-eight years. Both houses sent until my thirtieth. In my thirty-first the Order sent and the Brotherhood did not, and I held the Order to have broken nothing, for which the knight thanked me and gave me a number I had not asked for. In my thirty-second neither sent, and I read it to the Stone alone. There was a third at the reading, below the Stone in the ditch to the north, where neither house stands, hooded, who did not come up, and whose place in the ditch was dry after. The hollow holds more rain than it did. Agnet takes the roll.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: Read forty years, to the Stone, alone, aloud, because I was sworn to. The third stands in the ditch at every reading now and has come a pace nearer each thaw. I have measured. The ditch is not long enough for the paces it has taken. Last thaw it stood in the Stone's own shadow. I know what it is; the Reader of Stones at Kerrow knew; I have not written it and I will not. I will write that the ninth article did not say 'of ours' when I was sworn. It said 'of neither house', and the first keeper's note says so, and I read it last thaw as it stands now, aloud, because the oath is to read what is written, and I should have stopped there, and I read the two below, which were the Brotherhood's two when I was sworn and are not now, and[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Below, in a large unpractised hand: THE HUT WAS EMPTY AT THE THAW. THE ROLL WAS ON THE BENCH UNDER A STONE. THE READING WAS HEARD AT THE STONE THAT THAW BY THE CARTERS IN THE LANE, A WOMAN'S VOICE, THROUGH TO THE END, AND NOBODY STOOD ON THE STONE. I HAVE NOT READ THE TWO BELOW. I CANNOT READ.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]X.[/b] WHAT IS GIVEN TO HER IS GIVEN. SHE WASTES NOTHING.

[b]XI.[/b] THE HOLLOW IS FILLED. THE KEEPER TAKES HER SHARE LAST.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]First keeper: The two below the seals are the Brotherhood's, which asked eleven articles where the Order asked nine. The Order does not count them. The eleventh, when it was cut, said that the Maiden fills every hollow. I set that down because the Brotherhood's clerk asked me to witness the words, and I did.[/color][/i][/indent]

[b]Seals.[/b] For the Order, nine notches cut in the edge of the vellum with a knife, and a thumb of chrism, which is warm. For the Brotherhood, a short upright cut in the vellum with its lips drawn apart, and a thumb of blood, which has not dried.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Third keeper: There is a third seal under the two, at the foot, which I did not see made and which the two keepers before me do not mention: a ring of small cuts, fang-shaped, round a hollow pressed into the vellum. The hollow goes deeper than the vellum is thick. I have put my finger in it, to the knuckle, and the vellum lay flat on the bench.[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Survey of the Northern Walk
pages.by: Sent down to the Chapter-House on Reliquary Avenue in the year it bears; the chalk was at the Prior's lintel when I came for it, and the Prior had not read past the Fen.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] To the Prior of the Chapter-House on Reliquary Avenue, from the Reliquarist of the northern walk: the survey of the Hide as it stands in the three thousand three hundred and eleventh year of the Breath by the Order's count, which I use because the roads use it. Our own count the Prior has.

What we are for: to walk the Reliquary and write down what it holds, plainly, as it stands, since every house writes down what it would have it hold. I have walked from the Avenue up through the Chalk and the Dunes to the Jaw, and back by the Fen: nineteen weeks. The last survey of this walk is the Prior's own, nine years gone. I carried it and set my figures beside his. Where they differ I give both and do not choose.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Ashen Moor[/color][/font_size]

The ash is warm to the ankle in every season. The Prior gives the warmth at the Sighing Lantern as a hand held over coals; I give the same. The ground is not cooler than nine years ago. The ash-pickers say it is not cooler than in their grandmothers' time. The camps say it is the god cooling, and that it will cool. I set down that the Cooling, if that is what it is, has not moved in the memory of anyone I can ask, and that I do not know what a thing that cools so slowly is doing.

The camp at the Ashwake stones under Warden-Crone Esk: some forty tents, a smith, a healer, a vendor. Pilgrims going down. Nothing coming up but the knights' bone-carts.

Landmarks, as the Prior lists them. The Sighing Lantern: lit; it hums through its cracked bell when the breath is up, as before. The Widow's Stumps: three, warm, as before. The Broken Kneeler: two halves, unmoved. The Ashwake milestones: chalked by Villa Llaga's penitents, the chalk fresh. The waystone ring below the Jaw: eleven stones in the Prior's survey. I count eleven, and twelve, in turns.

The Hide showing through. The Prior listed four places on the Moor where the body breaks the turf: a rib standing out below the Jaw, a vein breaching the soil at the Ash Shore, a patch of skin with pores and coarse hairs on the Ridge, and a pool under the Widow's Stumps that looks back. I count seven. The three new: a second rib a span from the first, with marks cut on it which the ash-pickers call old and which were not there to be listed nine years ago; a knuckle, I think, breaking the Pilgrim Road at the second milestone, which the carts go round; and a second pool, beside the first, which looks at the first.

What is coming up. The ones who drank, which the camps call Husks, stand in rows in the ash where the god's blood runs out of it, and the black glass where they bleed is wider by the length of my cord than the Prior's line. The hands walk on their fingers at night, as before. The breath with mouths in it, as before. The kneeling ones: more. I counted a hundred and nine kneeling between the stones and the Jaw. The Prior counted ninety.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Rib Crypts[/color][/font_size]

Nine galleries between the ribs. The flagstones lift under the boot, slow and even; the Prior gives the interval as a long breath; I give it as a longer one. The Carrion Warden keeps the gate still, and does not salute. The Long Candle burns, and leans toward whoever comes near; it leaned toward me before I was in its gallery. The Weeping Rib weeps; the needles beneath it are more than can be swept. Sister Un's reliquary is gone, as it has always been, and no dust settles where it stood, and I set down that the place where it stood is a pace nearer the gate than the Prior's chart has it, and that the milestone which waits for it has moved too.

The Counting Wall. Tallies cut in groups of a hundred and eight, stopping mid-group, the counter having been interrupted, as everyone says. The Prior says that everyone who comes adds a mark. I did not. There is a mark more than the Prior's figure. Perhaps someone else.

The gate stair of the fourth gallery has nineteen steps going down and eighteen coming up. I went up and down it four times, counting, with my hand on the wall. I give both figures. I will not go down it again.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The catacombs[/color][/font_size]

The upper ossuary is as the pilgrims laid it, every wall a sermon in bone, the Wardens saluting one another in the corridors. The lower forgets its patterns a little higher up the stair than it did: the Prior marks the forgetting at the third landing; I mark it at the second. At the bottom the monks' pick is still in the end wall and the wall is still warm, and the warmth stands a hand higher up the shaft than the Prior's mark. I did not count the skulls in the Miscount. I know what the count does. The Matron keeps the lowest hall.

Of the book on the lectern in the upper ossuary I write at the end.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Barrows[/color][/font_size]

Two hundred and twelve lids by the Prior's count. Two hundred and twelve by mine, every one dished inward, and I did not count them twice. The Empty Ninth stands open. The Turned Mound has turned a quarter sunwise against the Prior's chart. The Grieving Stone: worn to a taper, warm, the rain in its hollow unfrozen; the keeper's hut beside it empty, with the door open, and no roll on the bench, and a stone on the bench where a roll would lie. The dead of Widow's Lane rise wrong, as before, more of them, and the lids lift at the dished hour a hand's breadth, all at once, and set down. Neither house contests them now. Both arrive after.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Drowned Fen[/color][/font_size]

The water does not wet. The Kneeling Arch leans forty degrees; I measured; forty. The Reed That Points Home turned, when I stood on the causeway, toward a village I do not know, which is not the Prior's village and is not mine, and I have set its bearing on the chart in case the Prior knows it. The Iron Hook has its doll. The bells under the square ring at dusk, and the belfry fell a thousand years ago; I heard them, and set down that they ring flat, by one breath, as the bells at Bellrest are said to. The House of the Fen gives its dead to the water and the Order's knights dredge them up and stand them, as before, and neither will speak to me of the other.

Below the Well-Shrine, the stilt-folk say, the Drowned Nave has a congregation, kneeling, and it has grown by one since the Prior's survey, and the one is a knight. I did not go down. I set down what is said.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Hollow Wood[/color][/font_size]

Pale trunks, warm a hand's depth in. Three colours of cap. Every tenth trunk holds something the god was carrying; I counted to the tenth and stopped, as the Prior did. The Ribcage Bough: the pilgrim's badge warm. The Niche Candle unrun. The Blind Face: the bark has grown a finger's width further over the eyes, and the mouth is a finger's width wider. I set down both measures. The Sword-in-Root: a hand's breadth more of the blade under the root than the Prior drew. The roots all lean toward the mouth of the Root Deep, which breathes, which I did not enter, by the Prior's instruction, and which breathed out as I came to its mouth and in as I left, and I was there a long while.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Burnt Heath[/color][/font_size]

Seven carcasses in the ring, facing the same way, the skull heaps as before. The ash in the middle of the ring, where the ground was opened once and closed, is soft, and warm, and dished, like a lid. My lantern would not go in. I went in. What I found there I will give the Prior at the Chapter-House and not on this leaf.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The Barrens beyond[/color][/font_size]

Off the Hide, on the white. The Dunes as the Prior gives them: bone ground fine, a day of walking on someone. The Valley of Standing Ribs: the Prior counted fifty-eight ribs, and the Order's brother who walked behind him wrote sixty-one under his. I counted sixty-one. A brother walked behind me and wrote sixty-four, and said my count would close in time, and asked my name, and I gave him the Prior's, and he wrote down a number. The Avenue: the bearers hold up their stone lanterns, every face toward the Chapter Stair; some lanterns are lit, and the Prior has never seen one lit, and nor have I, and there are more lit than nine years ago; the Halfway Kneeler kneels. The Chapter-House: the chalk at the lintels when I went up the Avenue nineteen weeks ago; at the second sills when I came down it. I ask the Prior whether the chapter digs, or goes to the Citadel. The Pale: I walked out along the white stones of the Order's line past the Dry Oasis; the Prior's chart ends the line at the hundred and third stone; I counted to the hundred and ninth and turned back, and the ground behind the stones was whiter than the ground ahead, and I did not go on to the hundred and tenth, which I could see.

The Socket. The Saint kneels where the joint was and has not finished his word. As before.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the count[/color][/font_size]

I set down, because the Prior asked for everything, that every count I took on this walk came out one higher the second time, except the Barrow lids, which I did not count twice; that at every fire I came to, one man was already sitting whom the camp could not say when it had seen arrive; and that in the Valley of Standing Ribs at dusk there was a thin one standing far off among the ribs with a finger up, moving it along the row, and that the Order's brother behind me saw it and said not to look, and said a word under his breath that I did not catch and will not ask for.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the book on the lectern[/color][/font_size]

In the upper ossuary, in the pilgrims' hall where the bone is laid as sermons, there is a lectern of bone with a book on it, open. The Prior's survey lists it: a book on a lectern, one page turned, the hand the reader's own. The Prior did not say what is written in it. I read it. I should not have. It was this survey, in my hand, from its first line to its last, through the Moor and the crypts, which I had not then walked, to the end, which I had not then written. It was a page ahead. Its last line was not in my hand. It was cut, in notches, a thumb apart.

I resolved at the lectern not to copy that line, since a thing copied is a thing kept, and I kept my resolve nineteen weeks and up the Avenue and down it and to the foot of this leaf, and I find now that I have one line left to write, and that it is the line, and that it is in my hand after all, since I am writing it. The Prior will know what to do with it. I do not. It is the count, as the book has it, for the year in which this survey is read.

Three thousand three hundred and twelve.
